title: If It Walks Like a Duck and Talks Like a Duck, Check to See If It’s an Aquaduck
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos, a teacher who is publicly pro science of reading but critical of its overreach, argues that the reading wars need more concessions and fewer caricatures. She says she is unapologetically supportive of Emily Hanford's reporting and of research-informed instruction, yet unreservedly critical of excessive phonics and misguided state legislation. She responds to anti science of reading Substack writers by noting that publishers profit from every side of the debate and that dismissing parents who simply want children taught to read amounts to gaslighting. Drawing on her own career, she credits balanced literacy for promoting wide reading and extensive writing while insisting that its unstructured phonics and predictable texts left many children behind. She holds up literacy coach Leah Mermelstein as a model of grey, nuanced thinking. Her conclusion is that educators should separate science from sales, lessons from legislators and research from reactionary politics.
points: Janetos holds two positions at once: strong support for science of reading research and sharp criticism of its excesses in phonics and legislation.
She argues both balanced literacy and science of reading publishers profit from the reading wars, and the same companies often own competing curricula.
Dismissing parents and teachers who demand research-informed instruction ignores the real experience of children left behind by earlier methods.
Balanced literacy deserves credit for wide reading and extensive writing even though its phonics instruction was unstructured.
The way forward is the habit of concession, acknowledging what each side got right instead of declaring winners and losers.
quotes: I am unapologetically pro-Emily Hanford’s reporting and pro-the science of reading movement. But I’m also unreservedly critical of overreach and overcorrection when I see it
Taking a side can sideline stuff that matters: centering text can sideline foundational skills; centering foundational skills can sideline reading text.
The winning side in the reading wars will be the side that allows humility to replace hubris, acknowledging what we got right and where we went wrong
Can we concede that the publishing companies cashing in on SOR are no different from the ones that cashed in on balanced literacy?
Balanced Literacy left too many students behind with unstructured phonics instruction and use of predictable text, but it was valuable in promoting wide-reading and extensive writing.
We need to stop the simplistic, ideologically-driven SOR bashing and objectively dissect the good, the bad, and the ugly of what the movement represents.
We need to separate science from sales, lessons from legislation, research from reactionary politics. We owe it to our students, their parents, and ourselves to go grey.
